title: PODCAST | The Spillover: How China Is Quietly Winning the Iran War Energy Crisis | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Five months into the Iran war, CFR's Sebastian Mallaby and Rebecca Patterson find equity markets strikingly calm even as oil prices climb again, and argue China has adapted best by cutting crude imports ~50% via stockpiled reserves and statist demand controls, while guest Kristian Coates Ulrichsen explains how Iran has effectively throttled the Strait of Hormuz through missile/drone deterrence alone, with no physical blockade needed.

themes.theme: Oil and market reaction to a five-month war

insights.claim: The Iran war began February 28, 2026 and, as of the August 2026 recording, shows no sign of ending; a June memorandum of understanding raised hopes of a peace deal but produced no lasting de-escalation.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Establishes the conflict as an extended, unresolved risk overhang on energy markets rather than a short-lived shock.
insights.quote: The Iran war, which began on February 28th, shows absolutely no sign of ending soon.
insights.locator: The Iran war, which began on February 28th

insights.claim: Brent crude was approaching $90 a barrel as of August 11, 2026, up from about $70 in early July when some analysts were calling a global oil supply glut, and well below the roughly $126 peak hit at the end of April.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Oil has round-tripped through a wide range within months — positioning and options strategies need to account for continued high realized volatility even as implied vol looks calm.
insights.quote: A barrel of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, is getting close to $90 again as of August 11th.
insights.locator: A barrel of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark

insights.claim: U.S. retail gasoline prices are staying above $4 a gallon, up from about $3 when the conflict started, and $4 is described as a psychological threshold that shows up quickly in consumer sentiment surveys and opinion polls ahead of the midterm elections.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Retail gasoline above the $4 psychological line is a political variable that could pressure the administration toward a faster, less favorable Iran settlement.
insights.quote: $4 a gallon is this psychological line in the sand. Anything above that, and you quickly hear about it in consumer sentiment surveys and in opinion polls
insights.locator: retail gasoline prices in the United States are staying above $4 a gallon

insights.claim: Equity market volatility has decoupled from geopolitical risk: the VIX has drifted back to pre-war levels even as a Federal Reserve-built geopolitical risk index (based on news mentions) remains elevated, close to its early-war highs.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: A visible gap between realized geopolitical risk and priced equity volatility is a potential mispricing — cheap tail-risk hedges may be available despite an unresolved war.
insights.locator: the geopolitical risk index created by two Federal Reserve researchers

insights.claim: Markets' reaction to Iran escalation has shrunk over time: in early March the Dow fell 2% on war escalation, but on July 13, when Trump announced reinstating the naval blockade on Iran and Brent jumped 9.5%, the Dow fell only about 0.3%.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: A concrete before/after data point showing equities have become desensitized to Iran escalation headlines even as oil still reacts sharply — a tradable divergence between equity and commodity vol.
insights.quote: when President Trump announced he was reinstating the naval blockade on Iran. That was enough to make the oil price, the Brent oil price jumped by 9.5%, but the Dow hardly moved. It was down like 0.3%.
insights.locator: you look at it today, more recently, like July 13

insights.claim: Gulf oil exports via pipeline rose from about 3 million barrels a day before the war to roughly 5-7 million barrels a day during it, as existing pipelines were used more aggressively to route around the closed Strait of Hormuz, still far below the roughly 20 million barrels a day that moved through the strait by ship pre-war.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Quantifies the real ceiling on pipeline workarounds — even maximized, they replace only a quarter to a third of pre-war Hormuz shipping volume.
insights.locator: at the start of the war, you had about 3 million barrels a day of Gulf oil exported via pipelines

insights.claim: Shipping companies have adapted by turning off transponders to try to move tankers through the Strait of Hormuz undetected.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Shadow-fleet-style evasion tactics are now active in the Gulf, complicating both sanctions enforcement and insurers' risk assessment of tanker movements.
insights.quote: you had ships turning off their transponders and so forth to try to sneak through in the dark
insights.locator: the shipping companies also got pretty cheeky

insights.claim: Western consumer countries led by Washington and Tokyo announced early in the war that they would release 2 million barrels a day from emergency stocks to offset the supply hit.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Coordinated strategic reserve releases were a first line of defense, but as later noted the U.S. reserve itself is now near multi-decade lows, limiting future firepower.
insights.locator: you had that announcement from the kind of Western consumers led by Washington and Japan

insights.claim: Between February and June 2026, China cut its crude oil imports by roughly half, about 5.5 million barrels a day, without a measurable hit to domestic economic growth.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: A halving of Chinese crude demand with no visible growth cost is a major, underappreciated bearish factor for oil prices and a template investors should watch China repeat in future shocks.
insights.quote: between February and June, China slashed its crude imports by fully half, so 5.5 million barrels a day.
insights.locator: the big surprise has been China

insights.claim: Analysts estimate China's roughly 50% cut in crude imports was by itself enough to shave about $30 off the price of Brent crude.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Gives a rough dollar-per-barrel sizing of China's single-country demand-destruction effect — useful for scenario-modeling Brent if China's import behavior reverses.
insights.quote: analysts think that that was enough by itself to have shaved maybe $30 off the price of Brent crude
insights.locator: to give you a sense, analysts think

insights.claim: China's ability to toggle oil imports up and down without suffering an economic slowdown makes it a 'swing consumer,' analogous to the swing-producer role Saudi Arabia and OPEC have historically played, and is reinforced because OPEC itself has been weakened by the UAE's secession.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Investors modeling oil-price sensitivity now need to treat Chinese import policy as a swing variable on par with OPEC production decisions.
insights.quote: China’s ability to toggle the imports up and down, without suffering an economic slowdown, makes China sort of a swing consumer
insights.locator: So China’s ability to toggle the imports up and down

insights.claim: An oil executive quoted in The Economist declared 'China is the new OPEC,' reflecting that China can adjust its oil imports essentially on the decision of one man, Xi Jinping, giving it fewer coordination problems than the 22 fractious members of OPEC+.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Centralized, single-decision-maker control over a demand lever this large is a structural advantage China holds that fragmented OPEC+ cannot match in a crisis.
insights.quote: a recent piece in The Economist quoted an oil executive saying, you know, China is the new OPEC.
insights.locator: And so a recent piece in The Economist

insights.claim: China bought about 200 million barrels for its strategic reserves in early 2026 when prices were moderating, then drew down roughly 70 million barrels of visible inventory by July (per data firm Vortexa), or an estimated 150 million barrels including floating storage and hidden caves — meaning China's net reserve position rose over the course of the war.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: China entered the war with a reserve cushion large enough that it came out of the first five months with more spare capacity than when it started — a key input for how long Beijing can sustain low imports.
insights.quote: China accumulated additional reserves in February of 200 million barrels, but only ran down 150 million barrels during the war.
insights.locator: By July, its inventories were down about 70 million barrels, according to Vortexa

insights.claim: Estimates suggest China could sustain another four months of full-on war at current import-cutting levels before Beijing would start to worry about its stock levels running low.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Gives investors a rough runway estimate for how long China's current low-import stance is sustainable absent a policy change.
insights.quote: The estimates I’ve seen suggest that China might be able to keep going for another four months of full-on war before Beijing really started to worry
insights.locator: The estimates I’ve seen suggest

insights.claim: China's economic resilience during the import cuts also came from its statist economy: the government ordered petrochemical plants to cut oil use, absorbed the hit using pre-existing excess petrochemical product stockpiles from industrial overcapacity, and cut exports of refined products like jet fuel, shifting adjustment costs onto trading partners.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: China's resilience isn't just reserves — it's centralized industrial-policy tools unavailable to market economies, meaning its demand response can be sustained through non-market channels too.
insights.locator: the government could order petrochemical plants to stop using oil

themes.theme: Systemic contrast: Chinese resilience vs. U.S. market efficiency

insights.claim: The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen below 300 million barrels, its lowest level since 1983, and cannot be drawn down to zero without risking damage to the physical infrastructure of the reserve system.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: The U.S. has materially less strategic reserve firepower left to deploy against a further Hormuz-driven price spike than it did entering the war.
insights.quote: We’re actually now at the lowest levels in reserves since 1983.
insights.locator: Just in the last week, the U.S. Department of Energy released a report

insights.claim: Market economies like the U.S. are very good at optimizing for efficiency through price signals in stable times, but the market system does not generate price signals that force resilience, insurance, or redundancy — that is a structural weakness relative to a statist system like China's.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: A framework for why the U.S. private sector systematically underinvests in strategic buffers (energy reserves, defense stockpiles) relative to China, relevant to any thesis about resilience-driven capex cycles.
insights.quote: what the market system doesn’t do is generate price signals that force you towards resilience, insurance, redundancy
insights.locator: But what the market system doesn’t do

insights.claim: U.S. politicians, facing frequent reelection, are structurally biased toward near-term voter-facing spending (welfare payments, mortgage interest deductions) rather than strategic insurance policies like energy reserves that may never be needed.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Explains a durable political-economy constraint on U.S. strategic reserve rebuilding — don't expect a rapid SPR refill driven by political incentives alone.
insights.locator: US politicians, you know, because they face reelection all the time

insights.claim: In a bad state of the world with elevated geoeconomic tensions, China's relative strength versus the United States increases, because its statist system plans for worst-case scenarios and insures against them in ways the U.S. private and public sectors do not.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: The overarching macro call of the episode: allocate for a widening China-U.S. resilience gap specifically during periods of geopolitical stress, even if U.S. systems outperform in calmer periods.
insights.quote: in a bad state of the world, with geoeconomic tensions left and right, China’s relative strength goes up a bit.
insights.locator: I just think, you know, just to sum that up

themes.theme: How the Strait of Hormuz has actually been closed

insights.claim: Iran has been able to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz without a physical blockade simply by launching missile and drone attacks on shipping, which spooks insurers into raising war-risk premiums and deters shippers from transiting — a much easier method than the mining tactics used in the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, when the strait was never fully closed.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: The mechanism of closure — deterrence via insurance/risk premium rather than physical blockade — means the strait can be reopened or reclosed quickly and cheaply by Iran, keeping the disruption risk persistent and hard to fully hedge away.
insights.quote: how easily Iran can throttle the Strait of Hormuz “simply by lobbing missiles and drones” and spooking insurers, with no physical blockade required
insights.locator: the most consequential development post February 28

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz is uniquely hard to route around because there is no alternative sea route in or out of the Persian Gulf; unlike Taiwan Strait or Strait of Malacca disruptions, there is no way to sail around Hormuz to reach the same destinations.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Explains why Hormuz disruption is structurally worse for global energy markets than other chokepoint risks — pipeline workarounds exist but remain within Iranian missile range, unlike a true maritime detour.
insights.quote: that’s actually what makes Hormuz unique among global choke points, is that there’s no other way around, at least by sea
insights.locator: And that’s actually what makes Hormuz unique

insights.claim: Qatar and Abu Dhabi have no pipeline workaround for liquefied natural gas exports, since their LNG facilities are entirely inside the Gulf, making them fully dependent on the Strait of Hormuz staying open.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: LNG exporters Qatar and Abu Dhabi carry Hormuz-closure risk with zero physical hedge, unlike crude producers who have partial pipeline redundancy.
insights.locator: there are no equivalent pipeline workarounds for liquefied natural gas

insights.claim: If Iran successfully negotiates a transit fee structure with Oman for the Strait of Hormuz, it would set a global precedent that other powers controlling local chokepoints could emulate — as seen when an Indonesian minister floated a similar fee idea for the Strait of Malacca before neighboring countries shut it down, citing binding obligations under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: A Hormuz fee precedent could trigger copycat chokepoint monetization attempts globally, raising structural shipping and insurance costs beyond the Middle East.
insights.quote: other powers learn from and seek to emulate as they try to turn their own local choke point waterway into some sort of advantage
insights.locator: that could be an example that, you know, other powers learn from

themes.theme: Contagion to other chokepoints and broader costs

insights.claim: A crisis in the Taiwan Strait would be less a throughput crisis than an output crisis: ships can reroute around Taiwan, but the strait's importance lies in the concentration of high-end chip manufacturing on both sides, and disrupting that could remove an estimated 5% of global GDP.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Distinguishes Taiwan Strait risk (industrial/output shock to chip supply chains) from Hormuz risk (pure transit shock), meaning hedges and second-order impacts differ materially between the two scenarios.
insights.quote: People estimate at least 5% of global GDP would be taken away by disrupting that manufacturing thing.
insights.locator: People estimate at least 5% of global GDP

insights.claim: The Red Sea route, via which Saudi Arabia has been exporting up to 5 million barrels a day through its east-west pipeline, is newly at risk as the 2022 truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis breaks down and Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping resume, which would force Saudi exports to reroute north through the Suez Canal at added time and cost.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: One of the war's key mitigating workarounds (the Saudi Red Sea route) is now itself at risk of closure, which would remove a major offsetting supply channel and could reintroduce upward oil-price pressure.
insights.locator: We have seen an increase in fighting in Yemen over the past month

insights.claim: Climate change is adding new chokepoint risk: a 2023-24 drought lowered Panama Canal water levels enough to force major rerouting of energy shipments from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia via Gibraltar, Suez, and the Red Sea, and a 2026 European heatwave is dropping Rhine and Danube river levels near record lows, affecting river transport.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Climate-driven chokepoint disruption is a growing, recurring risk layer on top of geopolitical chokepoint risk, likely to increase in frequency.
insights.locator: in 2023-24, there was a drought in Central America

insights.claim: If governments have to spend more on securing supply routes and chokepoints, that raises an unresolved fiscal question of how it gets paid for, at a time when defense budgets are already locked into multi-year legacy contracts that are slow to adapt even as warfare technology (cheap drones) changes quickly.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Mallaby
insights.so_what: Flags a coming fiscal-policy tension between rapid, cheap-drone-driven changes in warfare and slow-moving, contractually locked-in defense procurement — relevant to defense-sector capital allocation.
insights.quote: If governments have to spend more on security for supply routes, which it sounds from Kristian like that’s certainly a risk, how does it get paid for?
insights.locator: If governments have to spend more on security for supply routes
